To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neural circuitry that promotes wakefulness also contributes to emergence from anesthesia, and that this circuitry is not necessary for induction of general anesthesia.
(i) the hypocretin/orexin system is required for emergence from, but is dispensable for, induction of, anesthesia; and (ii) the hypocretins/orexins are required for normal sleep–wake behavior.

(i) a specific locus in the brain, the ventral preoptic area, is involved in the emergence from anesthesia, but not the induction of, general anesthetics, and (ii) the same locus is critical for the maintenance of wakefulness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms that control sleep and wakefulness, with the goal of developing novel treatments for sleep and wake disorders.
understanding the molecular basis for the sleep–wake switch and how it is perturbed by anesthetic chemicals.
understanding how the brain generates the conscious experience of pain and the neural basis of pain modulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural circuitry underlying emergence from anesthesia is similar to the neural circuitry regulating sleep–wake transitions.
sleep is not anesthesia and anesthesia is not sleep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that a brain region called the ventral tegmental area (VTA) is necessary for animals to emerge from anesthesia but not for induction.
we have identified a molecular mechanism for emergence from general anesthesia.
the neural circuitry that normally controls sleep–wake regulation also controls emergence from general anesthesia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain state of general anesthesia and sleep share common neural circuitry.
we have discovered a novel role for the orexin/hypocretin neuropeptide system in the regulation of the transition from unconsciousness to consciousness during emergence from general anesthesia (2).
